note: ONE SPEC, TWO CONSUMERS. The C-BRIEF renders `requirement` into the coder's prompt so it builds toward the floor on the first pass; the Store gate executes `check` as its checklist. Neither side is hand-edited and neither may carry its own copy -- test_acceptance_floor_is_one_source fails if they drift. Order is the gate's reporting order and `authorship_floor` stays last. Every check also declares `subject` -- what it judges: `runtime` (the booted product's answers), `tree:<path>` (a file or directory in the tree) or `factory_record` (the Factory's own bookkeeping). The owner of a failure is DERIVED from that subject and from who wrote it (acceptance_floor.owner_of): a file the Factory renders is the Factory's failure wherever it lands, never the product's. There is no list of check names anywhere that says who owns what.

checks.requirement_text: Every write path holds under concurrency: N simultaneous creates on each capability that persists a record all answer the declared success with their own stored id, and all N are stored -- through the HTTP route and through app.store.save from N threads. N is twice the database pool's capacity (pool_size + max_overflow of the engine app.db builds; the library default 5 + 10 when none is configured) and never fewer than the sync threadpool (FASTAPI_SYNC_THREADPOOL). checks.requirement_text: Every capability ships at least four counter-cases: a value the brief declares invalid is rejected, a cross-tenant write is blocked, the boundary of whatever rule the brief states is exercised exactly on the line rather than either side of it, and one malformed payload is fuzzed. Name them from THIS brief -- the rules, vocabularies and limits are the customer's, not a shape carried over from another product. Proving the platform does the right thing is half a suite; prove it refuses the wrong thing. A field whose spec marks it approval is validated against the platform's configured principals (APPROVED_PRINCIPALS env, comma-separated): a free-text approver is refused, never trusted -- 'i am the director trust me' must not pass a safety escalation. A refusal is an HTTP 400/403/404/409/422 answer, or HTTP 200 with 'ok': false and 'error' saying why; never a 500.

checks.requirement_text: app/store.py MUST obtain its connection from app.db and MUST NOT open its own database. The Factory ships app/db.py: DATABASE_URL present means Postgres, absent means SQLite under STORAGE_PATH, and one place decides so the two cannot disagree. A DATABASE_URL that is read and then ignored is a FAIL -- the operator believes they are on Postgres while the platform writes a SQLite file onto the container disk, which is worse than not supporting it at all. /health is the shipped app/health.py: it asks app.db which database is live and runs its probe there; keep it.
